I saw a question about bad breath that got me thinking that most people don't really know how to keep their mouth clean, healthy, and smelling fresh. Here are some best practices that will make you smell nice, avoid tooth decay, and help reduce the risk of health problems like heart disease (which chronic gum disease can contribute to due to inflammation).

Brushing

  • Brush twice daily

  • Use a medium bristle brush (soft doesn't remove enough grunk and firm can damage enamel)

  • For fronts and backs of teeth, hold brush at 45 degrees to teeth with the bristles pointed toward the gumline

  • Brushing should take a few minutes, evenly distributed across your teeth

  • Brush your tongue, even way back (this is critically important for good breath)

  • Use a fluoridated toothpaste with the ADA (or regional equivalent) seal of approval and generally avoid "whitening" toothpastes as they're bad for your teeth

  • Wait twenty minutes after eating or drinking to brush and vice versa. Doing either right after the other can damage enamel.

Flossing

  • It's annoying, but floss daily

  • Proper flossing involves cleaning under the gum on either side of each tooth; you're not just cleaning between teeth

  • Don't use waxed floss as it doesn't remove grunk as well. If your teeth are so tight the unwaxed stuff just shreds, waxed is better than nothing though

  • Bleeding the first few days is normal but ease up if it keeps going after that

Miscellaneous

  • Don't use mouthwash; it's generally not needed and bad for mouth health

  • Go get your teeth cleaned every six months to a year at the dentist. Opt for a flouride treatment, particularly if you don't have fluoridated drinking water or milk

  • Avoid whitening treatments that aren't from your dentist; a lot of the home kits and whitening shops can damage teeth

  • Chewing a xylitol gum after meals can help clean your teeth and increase saliva production to keep your mouth healthy

Ideally, get a tongue scraper for cleaning your tongue - does a much better job than the brush alone, I find.

Also, most mouthwashes are only marginally helpful at best, but I do find that gargling-and-swishing hydrogen peroxide (the diluted stuff you use to clean cuts and scrapes) actually helps a fair amount - just don't swallow it. It doesn't taste very good, but as long as you don't actually drink the stuff it's perfectly safe.
